title: Introduction to the preprocessor
recap: Before C++ compilation, the preprocessor handles directives and produces a translation unit. Includes insert other file content, while conditional directives decide which source text reaches the compiler.

A macro without replacement text can act as a build-time feature flag. Macro processing follows source order and is isolated to each translation unit unless a definition is introduced through an included file or compiler option.
objectives: Describe preprocessing as a stage before compilation.
Recognize the syntax and lifetime of preprocessor directives.
Use a feature macro with conditional compilation.
Exclude an inactive code path from the translation unit.
warnings: Preprocessor directives end at a newline rather than a semicolon.
The preprocessor does not understand C++ function or block scope.
A macro defined in one source file does not automatically affect another.
Replacement macros should not substitute for typed C++ constants or functions when safer alternatives exist.
challenge: Define ROOF_DIAGNOSTICS without replacement text. Always print the inspection status, conditionally print the sensor-bus diagnostic when that macro is defined, and keep a LEGACY_SENSOR diagnostic out of the compiled program because that macro is not defined.
hints: First, place the sensor-bus output inside a conditional block controlled by the already-defined ROOF_DIAGNOSTICS macro.

Pseudocode: DEFINE ROOF_DIAGNOSTICS with no replacement text. MAIN: always OUTPUT inspection status. IF ROOF_DIAGNOSTICS is defined, OUTPUT the sensor-bus diagnostic. END IF. IF LEGACY_SENSOR is defined, OUTPUT the legacy-sensor diagnostic. END IF. Return success. Do not define LEGACY_SENSOR.

Near-C++ structure: #define ROOF_DIAGNOSTICS int main() { std::cout << /* status line */; #ifdef ROOF_DIAGNOSTICS std::cout << /* sensor-bus line */; #endif #ifdef LEGACY_SENSOR std::cout << /* legacy-sensor line */; #endif /* return success */ }
